claims.source: The canonical activation mechanism outlined above, derived from the analysis of phosphorylated and unphosphorylated crystal structures of p38α (Zhang et al., 2011a) has recently been challenged by an NMR study of p38α in solution (Tokunaga et al., 2014), which surprisingly showed that the dual phosphorylation of the A-loop induces only small conformational changes to p38α, raising doubts about the reliability of conformational states associated with the canonical activation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a consequence of the NMR findings.

claims.claim: The study obtained a total sampling time of over 115 μs.
claims.source: In total, we obtained a high level of sampling (>115 μs) which allowed us to explore the molecular mechanism of p38α canonical activation in unprecedented detail and reconcile the apparently contradictory X-ray and NMR data.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of the computational work performed.

claims.claim: PT-metaD simulations were performed for human p38α in four different states: unphosphorylated, apo dually phosphorylated, dually phosphorylated with bound ATP-Mg2+, and dually phosphorylated with bound ATP-Mg2+ and MK2 docking peptide.
claims.source: We performed PT-metaD in the well-tempered ensemble to obtain free-energy surfaces (FESs) for human p38α in four different states: (1) the unphosphorylated, (2) the apo dually phosphorylated, (3) the dually phosphorylated state with bound ATP-Mg2+, and (4) the dually phosphorylated state with bound ATP-Mg2+ and MK2 docking peptide (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), obtaining total sampling times of 24.25, 24.85, 10.35, and 9.86 μs, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the simulation setup.

claims.claim: The total sampling times for the four states were 24.25, 24.85, 10.35, and 9.86 μs, respectively.
claims.source: We performed PT-metaD in the well-tempered ensemble to obtain free-energy surfaces (FESs) for human p38α in four different states: (1) the unphosphorylated, (2) the apo dually phosphorylated, (3) the dually phosphorylated state with bound ATP-Mg2+, and (4) the dually phosphorylated state with bound ATP-Mg2+ and MK2 docking peptide (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), obtaining total sampling times of 24.25, 24.85, 10.35, and 9.86 μs, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as quantitative data about the simulations.

claims.claim: When CV1 < 0.2 and CV2 > 0.8, the system assumes an inactive conformation.
claims.source: When CV1 < 0.2 and CV2 > 0.8, then the system assumes an inactive conformation (as in Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a definition of the collective variables.

claims.claim: When CV1 > 0.6 and CV2 < 0.2, the A-loop has formed the characteristic β-sheet motif and the enzyme has adopted the canonical active state.
claims.source: On the other hand, when CV1 > 0.6 and CV2 < 0.2, the A-loop has formed the characteristic β-sheet motif (as in Figure 1b) and the enzyme has adopted the canonical active state.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a definition of the collective variables.

claims.claim: The unphosphorylated p38α neither explores the active conformation, nor does it populate a state able to accommodate ATP.
claims.source: FES of the unphosphorylated state (upper left panel, Figure 2) and the representative structures of the explored minima (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, enlarged structures in Figure 2—figure supplement 2) show that the unphosphorylated protein neither explores the active conformation, nor does it populate a state able to accommodate ATP.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the FES analysis.

claims.claim: In the more inactive of the two free-energy minima of unphosphorylated p38α, the A-loop is positioned over the C-lobe forming contacts with residues involved in the substrate binding and phosphotransfer.
claims.source: Specifically, in the more inactive of the two free-energy minima - (CV1, CV2) = (0.2, 0.7) (upper left panel in Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), the A-loop is positioned over the C-lobe forming contacts with residues involved in the substrate binding and phosphotransfer (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the FES minima.

claims.claim: In the unphosphorylated p38α, the P-loop is quite flexible and the K53-E71 salt bridge is displaced from the C-lobe due to the broken regulatory spine.
claims.source: The P-loop is quite flexible and the K53-E71 salt bridge, which stabilizes ATP, is displaced from the C-lobe due to the broken regulatory spine that is otherwise formed with D168 upon ATP binding (Taylor and Kornev, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the unphosphorylated state.

claims.claim: E71 interacts with the MAPK-conserved R67 from the αC helix that stabilizes pT180 in the active form in over 90% of structures in the most populated cluster of unphosphorylated p38α.
claims.source: Furthermore, E71 interacts with the MAPK-conserved R67 from the αC helix that stabilizes pT180 in the active form (Figure 1b, present in >90% of structures in the most populated cluster).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the simulation data.

claims.claim: In the second minimum of unphosphorylated p38α, the A-loop contains a short helix which places the conserved R173 in direct contact with the K53-E71 salt bridge and D168 of the conserved DFG motif.
claims.source: On the other hand, the A-loop of the second minimum contains a short helix which places the conserved R173 in direct contact with the K53-E71 salt bridge, as well as D168 of the conserved DFG motif (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2b), while the P-loop is partly collapsed into the ATP-binding site.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the FES minima.

claims.claim: In both higher energy minima of unphosphorylated p38α, R173 is in contact with D168 which otherwise stabilizes ATP upon binding.
claims.source: We observe similar autoinhibitory interactions for the other two higher energy minima explored by p38α (Supplementary file 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2c,d). In both cases, R173 is in contact with D168 which otherwise stabilizes ATP upon binding (Kumar et al., 1995; Bellon et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claims.claim: One of the higher energy minima of unphosphorylated p38α explores a conformation reminiscent of the Src-like inactive conformation in which the A-loop forms a short helix stacked against the αC helix.
claims.source: Furthermore, in the more inactive minimum (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c), the P-loop is collapsed into the ATP-binding site; while the other explores a conformation reminiscent of the Src-like inactive conformation (Xu et al., 1999) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2d) in which the A-loop forms a short helix stacked against the αC helix.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation.

claims.claim: The Src-like inactive conformation has been previously observed in CDK and EGFR kinases.
claims.source: This configuration has been previously observed also in CDK (De Bondt et al., 1993) and EGFR kinases (Sutto and Gervasio, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claims.claim: The findings are in perfect agreement with experimental studies reporting that the unphosphorylated p38α shows almost no affinity for ATP.
claims.source: These findings are in perfect agreement with experimental studies reporting that the unphosphorylated p38α shows almost no affinity for ATP (Tokunaga et al., 2014; Frantz et al., 1998), confirming the strong regulation of the enzyme by phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: Ten 500-ns-long independent unbiased MD runs of unphosphorylated p38α at 380 K all quickly showed a change in the A-loop conformation toward the inactive state.
claims.source: We performed ten 500-ns-long independent runs at 380 K, all of which quickly showed a change in the A-loop conformation toward the inactive state and sampled conformations that fall in the regions explored in metadynamics simulations.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing unbiased MD simulations.

claims.claim: In one of the independent runs of unphosphorylated p38α, the A-loop managed to break the β-sheet motif, and the run was extended to 2.675 μs.
claims.source: Furthermore, in one of the independent runs the A-loop managed to break the β-sheet motif in the simulated time, so we extended this run to 2.675 μs to allow the protein to transition to the inactive state (Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing unbiased MD simulations.

claims.claim: In the extended unbiased MD run of unphosphorylated p38α, the protein mostly remained in the global minima observed in metadynamics simulations.
claims.source: Indeed, the protein mostly remained in the global minima observed in metadynamics simulations, and the final conformation showed very similar features to the representative inactive structures (Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing unbiased MD simulations.

claims.claim: RMSF reveal a high flexibility of several structural elements besides the A-loop (i.e. αC, αD, and the MKI helices) in unphosphorylated p38α that occurs due to the opening of the lobes and the local unfolding.
claims.source: Root-mean-square fluctuations (RMSF) reveal a high flexibility of several structural elements besides the A-loop (i.e. αC, αD, and the MKI helices, Figure 3b) that occurs due to the opening of the lobes and the local unfolding (in the case of αD helix).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on RMSF analysis.

claims.claim: Large conformational changes involving lobe opening and local unfolding have been previously linked to conformational changes in other kinases but have been so far unobserved for p38α.
claims.source: Both these events have been previously linked to large conformational changes occurring in other kinases (Sutto and Gervasio, 2013; Whitford et al., 2007; Shan et al., 2013) but have been so far unobserved for p38α.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claims.claim: Once p38α is dually phosphorylated, it explores conformations that are not largely different from the ones observed for the unphosphorylated protein, contrary to the reported X-ray data.
claims.source: Surprisingly, once p38α is dually phosphorylated, it explores conformations that are not largely different from the ones observed for the unphosphorylated protein (upper right panel in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, enlarged structures in Figure 2—figure supplement 3), contrary to the reported X-ray data (Zhang et al., 2011a).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on FES analysis with citation to X-ray data.

claims.claim: In the global minimum of dually phosphorylated p38α, the A-loop moves away from the ATP-binding site mostly due to the electrostatic interactions formed by the phosphorylated residues which also stabilize the P-loop.
claims.source: In the global minimum, the A-loop moves away from the ATP-binding site, mostly due to the electrostatic interactions formed by the phosphorylated residues which subsequently also stabilize the P-loop and prevent it from collapsing into the ATP binding pocket (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the FES.

claims.claim: In the global minimum of dually phosphorylated p38α, the sampled conformation is unlikely to bind ATP due to the formation of a salt bridge between R49 and D112.
claims.source: However, the sampled conformation is unlikely to bind ATP due to the formation of a salt bridge between R49 (positioned beneath the P-loop) and D112 (found at the beginning of the αD helix) (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3a; distance histogram is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the FES.

claims.claim: The R49-D112 interaction seems to be specific for the phosphorylated protein and locks the hinge and occludes the ATP-binding site.
claims.source: This interaction, which seems to be specific for the phosphorylated protein, locks the hinge and occludes the ATP-binding site.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the simulation data.

claims.claim: The dually phosphorylated p38α also explores a higher energy minimum that comes closer to the active one where the A-loop extends toward the L16 loop but does not form the β-sheet motif.
claims.source: However, the protein also explores a higher energy minimum that comes closer to the active one (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3b): the A-loop extends toward the L16 loop, yet does not form the β-sheet motif associated with the active conformation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on FES analysis.

claims.claim: In the higher energy minimum of dually phosphorylated p38α, the A-loop forms a number of electrostatic interactions with the αC helix and the L16 loop, while pT180 forms a salt bridge with R67.
claims.source: Regardless, the higher energy conformation allows the A-loop to form a number of electrostatic interactions with the αC helix and the L16 loop (Table 1), while pT180 forms a salt bridge with the highly conserved R67 preventing the P-loop from collapsing into the ATP-binding site.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the FES.

claims.claim: In the higher energy minimum of dually phosphorylated p38α, the αD helix partly unfolds allowing the ATP-binding pocket to assume a more open conformation with the key residues aligned for ATP binding.
claims.source: Furthermore, the αD helix partly unfolds allowing the ATP-binding pocket to assume a more open conformation with the key residues aligned for ATP binding.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the FES.

claims.claim: The observation explains the protein's low affinity toward ATP in the phosphorylated state.
claims.source: This observation explains the protein's low affinity toward ATP in the phosphorylated state (Tokunaga et al., 2014; Frantz et al., 1998) and demonstrates that the dual phosphorylation can help define a receptive ATP-binding site but is not sufficient for the protein to adopt the conformation captured by X-ray crystallography (Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: The dual phosphorylation can help define a receptive ATP-binding site but is not sufficient for the protein to adopt the conformation captured by X-ray crystallography.
claims.source: This observation explains the protein's low affinity toward ATP in the phosphorylated state (Tokunaga et al., 2014; Frantz et al., 1998) and demonstrates that the dual phosphorylation can help define a receptive ATP-binding site but is not sufficient for the protein to adopt the conformation captured by X-ray crystallography (Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the simulation data.

claims.claim: To populate the active state observed by X-ray crystallography, 16-18 kcal mol−1 of free energy would need to be added to the phosphorylated system.
claims.source: In fact, to populate that state, we would need to add 16–18 kcal mol−1 of free energy to the phosphorylated system (minimum located at (CV1, CV2) = (0.6, 0.2) in the upper right panel of Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3d).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on FES analysis.

claims.claim: Ten 1-μs-long independent unbiased MD runs of dually phosphorylated p38α at 380 K showed a change in the A-loop conformation toward the regions explored by the protein in metadynamics simulations.
claims.source: We performed ten 1-μs-long independent runs at 380 K, most of which showed a change in the A-loop conformation toward the regions explored by the protein in metadynamics simulations (upper right panel in Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing unbiased MD simulations.

claims.claim: In one of the independent runs of dually phosphorylated p38α, the A-loop broke the β-sheet motif, and the run was extended to 2 μs during which the protein settled in the higher energy minima likely to bind ATP.
claims.source: Furthermore, in one of the independent runs the A-loop broke the β-sheet motif, so we extended this run to 2 μs during which the protein settled in the aforementioned higher energy minima that seems likely to bind ATP (Figure 4a).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing unbiased MD simulations.

claims.claim: The FES plot for the phosphorylated system with bound ATP-Mg2+ complex shows a clear shift toward a more active conformation.
claims.source: The FES plot for the phosphorylated system with bound ATP-Mg2+ complex shows a clear shift toward a more active conformation (i.e. a displacement toward right and bottom in the lower left panel of Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, enlarged structures in Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on FES analysis.

claims.claim: The representative structure of the global minimum of phosphorylated p38α with bound ATP-Mg2+ does not form the β-sheet motif associated with the active state, but its A-loop extends toward the L16 loop and connects to the αC helix via the coordination of pT180 by R67 and R70.
claims.source: While the representative structure of the global minimum does not form the β-sheet motif associated with the active state (Figure 2—figure supplement 5a), its A-loop extends toward the L16 loop and connects to the αC helix via the coordination of pT180 by R67 and R70 (as observed in the active X-ray structure in Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the FES.

claims.claim: The β-sheet motif does form in the higher energy minimum of phosphorylated p38α with bound ATP-Mg2+, but pT180 forms less contacts with the αC helix and the L16 loop.
claims.source: The β-sheet motif does form in the higher energy minimum centered at (CV1, CV2) = (0.6, 0.1); however, its representative structure (lower left panel in Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 5b) shows pT180 forming less contacts with the αC helix and the L16 loop (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the FES.

claims.claim: The lack of interactions between pT180 and the αC helix/L16 loop, together with the disorder present in the P-loop, breaks the contact of E71 with Mg2+ ions resulting in a less stable complex with ATP.
claims.source: The lack of these interactions, together with the disorder present in the P-loop, breaks the contact of E71 with Mg2+ ions resulting in a less stable complex with ATP.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the FES.

claims.claim: The binding of ATP stabilizes an active-like structure, but it is not enough for the protein to display the active conformation observed in the crystal structure.
claims.source: Overall, albeit the binding of ATP stabilizes an active-like structure, it is not enough for the protein to display the active conformation observed in the crystal structure (Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the simulation data.

claims.claim: Ten 1-μs-long independent runs of dually phosphorylated p38α with bound ATP-Mg2+ at 380 K were performed, and most simulations explored only the local minimum close to the starting structure.
claims.source: We performed ten 1-μs-long independent runs at 380 K of the dually phosphorylated p38α with bound ATP-Mg2+ starting with the A-loop in the extended conformation (as in Figure 1b) (see Materials and methods). Most of the simulations explored only the local minimum close to the starting structure, while one of the runs showed more conformational diversity, so we extended it to 1.55 μs which allowed the protein to transition to the global minimum (Figure 5a).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing unbiased MD simulations.

claims.claim: In the extended unbiased MD run of dually phosphorylated p38α with bound ATP-Mg2+, the final conformation shows the disruption of the β-sheet motif in the A-loop.
claims.source: The final conformation shows the disruption of the β-sheet motif in the A-loop and the calculated RMSFs reveal its high flexibility (Figure 5b).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing unbiased MD simulations.

claims.claim: RMSF values show a lower flexibility of the protein upon the addition of ATP compared to the simulations of the apo systems.
claims.source: Overall, RMSF values show a lower flexibility of the protein upon the addition of the ATP compared to the simulations of the apo systems (Figures 3b and 4b).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on RMSF analysis.

claims.claim: The binding of the MK2 docking peptide could provide the necessary stability to form the β-sheet motif in dually phosphorylated p38α with bound ATP-Mg2+.
claims.source: While the dual phosphorylation and the ATP-binding drive the enzyme toward an active conformation, there is an obvious need for additional elements to complete the transition. Particularly, we wondered whether the binding of the MK2 docking peptide could provide the necessary stability to form the β-sheet motif.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a hypothesis tested by the simulations.

claims.claim: The FES for dually phosphorylated p38α with bound ATP-Mg2+ and MK2 docking peptide shows a deepening of the minimum associated with the formed β-sheet motif.
claims.source: The FES for this system indeed shows a deepening of the minimum at (CV1, CV2) = (0.7, 0.1) which is associated with the formed β-sheet motif (lower right panel in Figure 2, enlarged structures in Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on FES analysis.

claims.claim: In the representative structure of the minimum with formed β-sheet motif in the presence of MK2 peptide, pT180 is near the three conserved arginines (R67, R70, and R173), while pY182 displays higher mobility and moves away from H228.
claims.source: The representative structure of the minimum (Figure 2—figure supplement 6a) confirms this observation and shows pT180 near the three conserved arginines (R67, R70, and R173), while pY182 again displays higher mobility and moves away from H228 (Table 1, Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the FES.

claims.claim: The addition of the MK2 peptide does not eliminate the global minimum observed in the presence of ATP, but it flattens the FES which would indicate an easier transition between the two minima.
claims.source: Furthermore, the addition of the MK2 peptide does not eliminate the global minimum at (CV1, CV2) = (0.4, 0.4), observed also in the presence of ATP (two lower panels in Figure 2). However, it flattens the FES which would indicate an easier transition between the two described minima.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on FES analysis.

claims.claim: Ten 1-μs-long independent unbiased MD runs of dually phosphorylated p38α with bound ATP-Mg2+ and MK2 docking peptide at 380 K were performed, obtaining a total accumulated sampling time of 10 μs.
claims.source: In addition, we performed unbiased MD simulations of the dually phosphorylated p38α with bound ATP-Mg2+ and the MK2 docking peptide. We generated ten 1-μs-long independent runs at 380 K, obtaining a total accumulated sampling time of 10 μs (see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing unbiased MD simulations.

claims.claim: In the unbiased MD simulations with MK2 peptide, the protein remains mostly in the regions associated with the extended conformation of the A-loop with formed β-sheet motif, but also explores the conformational space closer to the other global minimum.
claims.source: The protein remains mostly in the regions associated with the extended conformation of the A-loop with formed β-sheet motif, but it also explores the conformational space closer to the other global minimum (also the global minimum in the system without the MK2 peptide) (Figure 6a).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing unbiased MD simulations.

claims.claim: The N-terminal part of the MK2 docking peptide binds the ED site and stabilizes the αD-αE linker hindering the flexibility of the αD helix and allowing D112 to reorient and stabilize ATP by forming hydrogen bonds with ribose.
claims.source: Interestingly, the N-terminal part of the MK2 docking peptide binds the ED site and stabilizes the αD-αE linker hindering the flexibility of the αD helix and allowing the D112 to reorient and stabilize ATP by forming hydrogen bonds with ribose (Figure 2—figure supplement 6, Figure 6b).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the unbiased MD simulations.

claims.claim: The D112-ATP interaction is more stable in the presence of the MK2 peptide than in its absence, which explains the phosphotransfer enhancement upon MK2 peptide docking.
claims.source: While we also observe this interaction in the absence of the MK2 peptide, it is not as stable as in its presence which explains the phosphotransfer enhancement upon MK2 peptide docking (Tokunaga et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to experimental study.

claims.claim: p38α predominantly samples conformations with the fully extended A-loop only upon double phosphorylation and the binding of ATP and the docking peptide.
claims.source: Our results suggest that p38α predominantly samples conformations with the fully extended A-loop only upon double phosphorylation and the binding of ATP and the docking peptide.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the simulation data.

claims.claim: Careful analysis of the crystal contacts in the X-ray structure of dually phosphorylated p38α reveals numerous interactions formed between functionally important structural elements, such as the L16 loop.
claims.source: However, careful analysis of the crystal contacts (which form between the molecules due to their orientation and packing within the crystal, Figure 7) reveals numerous interactions formed between functionally important structural elements, such as the L16 loop.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the crystal structure.

claims.claim: An atypically long expression His-tag of a neighboring molecule is bound to the hydrophobic docking groove in the crystal structure, which has the same effect on the protein as the MK2 docking peptide.
claims.source: Particularly, we found an atypically long expression His-tag of a neighboring molecule bound to the hydrophobic docking groove which, upon closer inspection (see below), has the same effect on the protein as the MK2 docking peptide did in our simulations.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the crystal structure.

claims.claim: A crystal supercell simulation of apo dually phosphorylated p38α composed of 4 unit cells and 16 protein molecules was performed, obtaining 8 μs of sampling for ~170,000 atoms.
claims.source: To prove that this is the case, we simulated a crystal supercell of the apo dually phosphorylated p38α composed of 4 unit cells and 16 protein molecules (see Materials and methods), which allowed us to maintain crystal contacts and obtain 8 μs of sampling for ~170,000 atoms.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the crystal simulation.

claims.claim: In the crystal supercell simulation, the A-loop is very stable in the conformation captured by the X-ray model - the β-sheet motif is unperturbed during the simulation, as well as the contacts made by pT180 with the three conserved arginines.
claims.source: As shown by Figure 8, the A-loop is very stable in the conformation captured by the X-ray model - the β-sheet motif is unperturbed during the simulation, as well as the contacts made by pT180 with the three conserved arginines (R67, R70, and R173).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the crystal simulation.

claims.claim: In the crystal supercell simulation, pY182 is more mobile and at times breaks away from H228 and the conserved arginines of the P+1 loop, which is consistent with the electron density.
claims.source: However, pY182 is more mobile and at times breaks away from H228 and the conserved arginines of the P+1 loop (R186 and R189). This is consistent with the electron density which is not so well defined for pY182 as it is for the rest of the A-loop.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the crystal simulation and comparison with experimental data.

claims.claim: The B-factors from the crystal simulation could be qualitatively matched with those reported for the X-ray structure.
claims.source: Furthermore, we could also qualitatively match the B-factors reported for the X-ray structure (PDB ID: 3PY3) (Figure 8b,d), while the most mobile regions in our simulations (mainly, the N- and C-terminal tails) are missing from the deposited electron density.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on comparison of simulation and experimental data.

claims.claim: The deposited crystal structure does not fully capture the apo conformation that p38α assumes under physiological conditions and it most likely suffers from artifacts due to the crystal contacts.
claims.source: Thus, our analysis and simulations strongly suggest that the deposited crystal structure does not fully capture the apo conformation that p38α assumes under physiological conditions and it most likely suffers from artifacts due to the crystal contacts.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the crystal simulation analysis.

claims.claim: p38α never explores the αC-out conformation in which the helix rotates by >45°, unlike CDK5, EGFR, and Src.
claims.source: Unlike CDK5 (Berteotti et al., 2009), EGFR (Sutto and Gervasio, 2013), and Src (Shukla et al., 2014; Foda et al., 2015), p38α never explores the αC-out conformation (neither in any of the deposited X-ray structures - Figure 9a nor in our simulations), in which the helix rotates by >45° (breaking the K53-E71 salt bridge in the process).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to other kinase studies.

claims.claim: The lack of αC-out conformation in p38α likely occurs due to the extensive range of contacts formed between the αC and the L16 helix, which is unique to MAPKs.
claims.source: This likely occurs due to the extensive range of contacts formed between the αC and the L16 helix, which is unique to MAPKs, indicating that the observed feature could be family-specific.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an explanation based on structural features.

claims.claim: MAP kinases contain two conserved arginine residues (R67 and R70) in the αC helix that readily form salt bridges with numerous negatively charged residues in the A-loop.
claims.source: Furthermore, MAP kinases contain two conserved arginine residues (R67 and R70) in the αC helix that readily form salt bridges with numerous negatively charged residues in the A-loop (Figure 10), thereby stabilizing various A-loop conformations which are not necessarily observed by X-ray crystallography.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the simulation data.

claims.claim: Just 47 out of 206 structures of human p38α in the PDB have complete A-loops without any missing or zero-occupancy residues.
claims.source: Despite an overwhelming amount of structural data (with 206 structures of human p38α in the PDB), just 47 structures have complete A-loops (i.e. without any missing or zero-occupancy residues), out of which only one structure contains the A-loop devoid of any crystal contacts (PDB ID: 2BAJ).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on analysis of PDB structures.

claims.claim: The lack of complete A-loop information in most structures indicates how flexible the A-loop is and why it is almost impossible to resolve it unless it forms crystal contacts.
claims.source: However, the mere lack of information indicates just how flexible the A-loop is and why it is almost impossible to resolve it unless it forms crystal contacts.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the structural data.

claims.claim: The unphosphorylated p38α never explores a conformation that could possibly bind and stabilize ATP mostly due to A-loop interactions with the DFG-Asp which is crucial for ATP stabilization.
claims.source: Our extensive simulations also indicate that the unphosphorylated p38α never explores a conformation that could possibly bind and stabilize ATP - mostly due to A-loop interactions with the DFG-Asp which is crucial for ATP stabilization (Kumar et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation.

claims.claim: Related proteins like ERK2 are able to bind ATP in the unphosphorylated state most likely due to longer A-loops.
claims.source: It is worth noting that related proteins, like ERK2, are able to bind ATP in the unphosphorylated state (Lee et al., 2005; Sours et al., 2008; Canagarajah et al., 1997; Khokhlatchev et al., 1998) most likely due to longer A-loops (Figure 10), which are then easier to stabilize away from the ATP-binding site.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation changes the free-energy surface and enables the A-loop to form salt bridge interactions with the autoinhibitory arginine residues R67 and R173.
claims.source: Phosphorylation, however, does change the free-energy surface and enables the A-loop to form salt bridge interactions with the autoinhibitory arginine residues - R67 and R173.

results.result: The study employed extensive parallel tempering metadynamics (PT-metaD) simulations totaling over 115 μs of sampling time across four different states of p38α (unphosphorylated, apo dually phosphorylated, dually phosphorylated with ATP-Mg2+, and dually phosphorylated with ATP-Mg2+ and MK2 peptide), with individual sampling times of 24.25, 24.85, 10.35, and 9.86 μs respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 provide clear quantitative data about the computational sampling performed. The total sampling time exceeds 115 μs as stated, and the individual sampling times for each system are explicitly reported. The methodology is well-documented in the Materials and Methods section, and convergence criteria are described.

results.result: Unphosphorylated p38α does not explore active conformations or ATP-binding competent states. The A-loop adopts autoinhibitory conformations with interactions between R173 and D168 (the DFG-Asp crucial for ATP stabilization), and the P-loop is flexible or collapsed into the ATP-binding site. These findings are consistent with experimental observations of negligible ATP affinity in the unphosphorylated state.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C44 and C86 collectively describe the conformational behavior of unphosphorylated p38α based on FES analysis and unbiased MD simulations. The structural features are well-characterized, including specific residue interactions (Table 1), RMSF analysis showing flexibility, and comparison with experimental ATP-binding data (C39). The extended 2.675 μs unbiased MD simulation (C41-C42) provides validation of the metadynamics results. The comparison with other kinases (C37-C38, C44) is appropriately cited.

results.result: Dual phosphorylation of p38α does not induce the large conformational changes observed in X-ray structures. Instead, the phosphorylated protein explores conformations not largely different from the unphosphorylated state, with the ATP-binding site occluded by a novel R49-D112 salt bridge. A higher energy minimum (~4-6 kcal/mol) shows a more open ATP-binding pocket but still lacks the β-sheet motif. The active X-ray conformation would require 16-18 kcal/mol of free energy, explaining the low ATP affinity observed experimentally.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C56, C88, C91-C92 describe the surprising finding that phosphorylation alone is insufficient for activation. The FES analysis clearly shows the energy landscape, the R49-D112 interaction is documented with distance histograms (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), and the 2 μs extended unbiased MD simulation (C56) validates the metadynamics results. The findings are consistent with experimental ATP-binding affinity data (C52, C92). The identification of the R49-D112 salt bridge as a phosphorylation-specific autoinhibitory interaction is a novel mechanistic insight.

results.result: ATP-Mg2+ binding shifts the free-energy landscape toward more active conformations, with the A-loop extending toward the L16 loop and forming contacts with R67 and R70. However, ATP binding alone is insufficient to stabilize the fully active conformation observed in crystal structures. The β-sheet motif forms in a higher energy minimum but with reduced contacts between pT180 and the αC helix/L16 loop, resulting in less stable ATP coordination.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C64 and C96 describe the effect of ATP binding based on FES analysis and unbiased MD simulations. The 1.55 μs extended simulation (C62-C63) shows transition to the global minimum, validating the metadynamics results. The structural analysis is detailed with specific residue interactions, and RMSF analysis (C64) shows reduced flexibility compared to apo systems. The conclusion that ATP binding is insufficient for full activation is consistent with NMR data (C96).

results.result: The MK2 docking peptide is required for p38α to predominantly sample the fully active conformation with the extended A-loop and β-sheet motif. The peptide stabilizes the αD-αE linker through binding at the ED site, allowing D112 to reorient and stabilize ATP through hydrogen bonds with ribose. This explains the experimentally observed 20-fold increase in ATP-binding affinity and enhancement of phosphotransfer upon peptide binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C73 and C97-C99 describe the critical role of the MK2 peptide in achieving full activation. The FES shows deepening of the active minimum (C66), and 10 μs of unbiased MD simulations (C69-C70) validate the stability of the active conformation. The mechanistic insight about D112 stabilization of ATP (C71-C72) is supported by distance histograms (Figure 6b) and is consistent with experimental phosphotransfer enhancement data. The hypothesis about the peptide preventing R49-D112 interaction (C98) is reasonable based on the structural data.

results.result: The X-ray crystal structure of dually phosphorylated p38α (PDB: 3PY3) contains extensive crystal contacts, including an atypically long His-tag from a neighboring molecule bound to the hydrophobic docking groove, which mimics the effect of the MK2 peptide. Crystal supercell simulations (8 μs, ~170,000 atoms) show that these contacts stabilize the active conformation observed in the crystal, suggesting the deposited structure does not fully represent the physiological apo conformation and likely suffers from crystallization artifacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C80 provide a critical reanalysis of the X-ray structure. The crystal contact analysis (Figure 7) is thorough, identifying specific interactions including the His-tag binding. The crystal supercell simulation is technically sophisticated and provides 8 μs of sampling that validates the stability of the X-ray conformation under crystal packing constraints. The B-factor comparison (C79) shows qualitative agreement, and the authors appropriately discuss limitations of quantitative B-factor comparison due to temperature differences and ensemble averaging. This analysis explains the discrepancy between X-ray and NMR data.

results.result: Unlike other kinases (CDK5, EGFR, Src), p38α never explores the αC-out conformation where the αC helix rotates by >45°. This is likely due to extensive contacts between the αC helix and the L16 helix, which is unique to MAPKs. Additionally, MAPKs contain two conserved arginine residues (R67 and R70) in the αC helix that form salt bridges with negatively charged A-loop residues, stabilizing various conformations.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 describe MAPK-specific structural features based on simulation data and comparison with other kinases. The absence of αC-out conformation is documented in both simulations and X-ray structure analysis (Figure 9a). The explanation based on αC-L16 contacts is structurally reasonable. The role of R67 and R70 is supported by the simulation data showing their interactions throughout different states.

results.result: Analysis of 206 human p38α structures in the PDB reveals that only 47 have complete A-loops without missing or zero-occupancy residues, and only one structure (PDB: 2BAJ) has an A-loop devoid of crystal contacts. This lack of complete structural information indicates the high flexibility of the A-loop and the difficulty in resolving it crystallographically unless stabilized by crystal contacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 provide a systematic analysis of available structural data. The quantitative assessment of PDB structures is verifiable and supports the conclusion about A-loop flexibility. This analysis strengthens the argument that crystal structures may not fully represent solution conformations.

results.result: Related proteins like ERK2 can bind ATP in the unphosphorylated state, most likely due to longer A-loops that are easier to stabilize away from the ATP-binding site.
results.evaluation: Claim C87 provides a comparative analysis with appropriate citations. The sequence alignment (Figure 10) supports the observation about A-loop length differences. The explanation is reasonable but remains somewhat speculative as it's based on inference rather than direct simulation of ERK2.

results.result: The MAPK-specific residue R67 is functionally important, as evidenced by the R67A mutation decreasing p38α kinase activity and the R67I somatic mutation found in colon adenocarcinoma.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 cite experimental and clinical data supporting the functional importance of R67. The mutation data from the literature and COSMIC database provide independent validation of the computational findings about R67's role.

results.result: The R49-D112 salt bridge observed in simulations appears inconsistent with X-ray structures where these residues are ~15 Å apart. However, R49 is part of a flexible loop below the P-loop (often unresolved in structures) and frequently interacts with E160 in simulations (~9 Å in X-ray structures). The discrepancy likely arises because the loop containing R49 forms crystal contacts in all 206 deposited structures, restricting its mobility.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 address a potential criticism of the R49-D112 interaction by providing a detailed analysis of X-ray structures and explaining the discrepancy. The distance analysis (Figure 9b,c) supports the explanation. The observation that R49's loop forms crystal contacts in all structures is a strong argument for why this interaction hasn't been observed crystallographically. The authors appropriately acknowledge the apparent discrepancy and provide a reasonable mechanistic explanation.

results.result: The study provides the first molecular-level description of how different regulators (phosphorylation, ATP, docking peptide) affect p38α enzymatic activity and reconciles the seemingly contradictory X-ray and NMR data through an integrative picture of the activation mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5 and C100-C101 represent the overarching conclusions of the study. The extensive simulation data (>115 μs total sampling) across multiple states, combined with validation through unbiased MD and crystal simulations, support these conclusions. The study successfully explains why NMR shows small conformational changes upon phosphorylation (consistent with the simulation results) while X-ray shows large changes (explained by crystal artifacts). The mechanistic insights about the sequential requirements for activation (phosphorylation → ATP → docking peptide) are well-supported by the data.

results.result: The collective variables (CVs) used in the study are defined such that CV1 < 0.2 and CV2 > 0.8 corresponds to an inactive conformation, while CV1 > 0.6 and CV2 < 0.2 corresponds to the canonical active state with the β-sheet motif formed.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 define the collective variables used for the metadynamics simulations. The definitions are clear and based on contact maps from reference inactive and active structures. This is a standard approach for studying protein kinase conformational changes.

results.result: Background information establishes that p38α is a therapeutically important Ser/Thr kinase with a complex structure and activation mechanism. Despite decades of research, the molecular mechanism of activation remains unclear, with recent NMR data challenging the X-ray crystallography-based canonical activation model.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C25 provide background information with appropriate citations. These claims establish the biological importance of p38α, describe its structural features, and identify the key scientific question (discrepancy between X-ray and NMR data) that motivates the study. All statements are properly referenced to the literature.
